title: How to Organize Your Real Estate Contacts (Phone, Gmail, Sheets)
summary: A step-by-step way to pull your real estate contacts out of your phone, Gmail and spreadsheets, remove duplicates, and sort your sphere into A, B and C lists.
body_markdown:
Ask most agents how many people are in their sphere and you'll get a shrug and a number that's off by a thousand.


That's because the database isn't in one place. Some of it lives in your iPhone. Some is in Gmail, including people you emailed once and never saved. There's a spreadsheet from your first year, an export from a brokerage CRM you stopped using, and a stack of open house sign-in sheets in the car. Nobody can work a sphere spread across six places.


This walkthrough gets it into one list, cleaned up and tiered, so you know who to call this week. Plan on a weekend for a database of a few thousand names, and less if you're newer. If you want to know what to do with the list once it's clean, our[guide to building and maintaining your sphere of influence](https://getdex.com/blog/real-estate-sphere-of-influence/) picks up from there.


**Fast facts:**


-


Your contacts are probably split across your phone, email, a spreadsheet and some kind of CRM.


-


Gmail quietly saves everyone you've emailed under "Other contacts." It's often the biggest pile you've never looked at.


-


iPhone's duplicate finder only catches contacts with identical names. "Mike Torres" and "Michael Torres" slip through.


-


Google Contacts' "Merge & fix" can't merge contacts stored in two different Google accounts.


-


A simple A/B/C split covers most agents. Roughly a tenth of your sphere should be on your A list.


*Image: A sphere sorted into columns on a board view in Dex*


## Step 1: Find every place your contacts live


Before you clean anything, make a list of the sources. Here's where agents' contacts usually hide and how to get them out.


Source


What's usually in it


How to get it out


iPhone (iCloud)


Clients, friends, family, vendors, everyone who's ever called you


On iCloud.com, open Contacts, select all, and export as vCard. Or connect the phone directly to the tool you're moving to.


Google Contacts


People you saved from Gmail or an Android phone


contacts.google.com, then Export, then Google CSV


Gmail "Other contacts"


Everyone you've emailed but never saved: lenders, inspectors, clients from years ago


In Google Contacts, open "Other contacts" in the left menu. Select the people worth keeping and add them to contacts first.


A second Gmail or Outlook account


Your old brokerage email, a personal account


Export each one separately


Brokerage or team CRM


Past transactions, close dates, portal inquiries


Look for a CSV export in settings. If you can't find it, ask your admin now, not after you leave.


Spreadsheets


Your first-year sphere list, mailing lists, holiday card lists


Save as CSV


Paper (open house sheets, business cards)


Neighbors, buyers who weren't ready, vendors


Scan the cards with a phone app, type the sheets in once, then recycle them


Facebook and LinkedIn


People who know what you do but never got saved anywhere


Leave these for last. Pull in only the people you'd actually reach out to.


The brokerage CRM row matters more than it looks. If your past transactions only exist in software your brokerage pays for, you may lose them when you switch firms. Get a copy of your data while you still have access, even if you have no plans to leave.


## Step 2: Pick one home and bring everything in


Choose where your database will live from now on. It can be Google Contacts, a spreadsheet or a CRM, but it has to be one place. The rest become sources you import from once and then stop using.


Whatever you choose should sync with your phone, because that's where new numbers get added during the day. Without a sync you'll be copying numbers by hand forever.


Before you start merging, put every CSV and vCard export in one folder and leave it alone. If a merge goes wrong, you can go back.


## Step 3: Merge duplicates


Once everything is in one place, you'll have duplicates. A lot of them. The same client saved as "Jen Park," "Jennifer Park" and "Jen (Maple St buyer)."


Each tool has its own merge feature and its own blind spot:


Tool


Where to find it


What it misses


iPhone Contacts


"Duplicates Found" under your own card at the top of the list. Tap View Duplicates, then Merge All or one at a time.


Only matches identical names. Won't catch nicknames, middle initials or a contact saved in both iCloud and Gmail.


Google Contacts


Menu, then "Merge & fix." Merge one at a time or Merge all.


Can't merge contacts stored in two different Google accounts.


Google Sheets or Excel


Sort by email, then by phone. Duplicates end up next to each other.


Only finds exact matches, so clean up phone formats first. (555) 123-4567 and 555.123.4567 won't match.


A CRM


Usually a duplicates or merge screen


Varies. Check whether merging can be undone before you click "merge all."


Run the automatic merge first, then scan by last name for the near-misses. Nicknames are the big one: Bob and Robert, Liz and Elizabeth, Mike and Michael. Couples are the other. Decide now whether a married couple is one record or two. One record per person is usually better, linked to each other, because they don't always text you from the same phone.


## Step 4: Archive the people you'd never call


Agents skip this step because it feels like throwing business away, but it isn't. A database with 4,000 names where 2,500 are noise means you'll never work it.


Archive, don't delete. You want them out of your daily view, not gone forever. Good candidates:


-


Vendors you've stopped using and agents you met once at a class


-


Wrong numbers, numbers with no name, and "Pizza place"


-


Portal inquiries from years ago who never replied


-


People you couldn't place if they called you tomorrow


A useful test: if this person called you right now, would you know who they are? If not, and there's nothing in the record to tell you, archive them.


## Step 5: Sort your sphere into A, B and C lists


Now tier what's left. Don't overthink it. You should be able to tier each contact in a few seconds.


Tier


Who belongs here


Rough share of your sphere


How often to reach out


A list


Past clients who've referred you or clearly would, close friends who send business, your best referral partners


About 10%


Monthly, plus their personal dates and a pop-by or two a year


B list


Past clients you're on good terms with, friends and neighbors who know what you do


About 30%


Every two to three months, plus close anniversaries and birthdays


C list


Acquaintances, people from open houses, old colleagues


The rest


A few times a year, mostly by email


Some agents add a D tier for people they're unsure about. If you're unsure, put them on C. A tier is a guess about the next year, not a permanent label, so move people up when they send a referral and down when they stop replying.


For how many touches each tier should get and when, see our[33 Touch plan, updated with tiers](https://getdex.com/blog/33-touch-plan/) .


## Step 6: Add the few fields that matter


A name and number is a contact. A name, number and close date is a past client you can actually stay in touch with. Here's what's worth adding, and what isn't.


Field


Why it matters


Who needs it


Relationship type (past client, sphere, referral partner, agent, vendor)


Lets you filter for the right people when you send something


Everyone


Tier (A, B, C)


Tells you how often to reach out


Everyone


Close date


Sets up the anniversary text every year


Past clients


Property address


Lets you send sales on their street, and map your past clients


Past clients


Referral source


Shows you who sends you business


Anyone who came from a referral


One personal detail (kids, pets, a hobby, something from the deal)


Makes your next message sound like you know them


A and B lists


Skip fields you won't keep up. "Last contacted" typed by hand will be wrong within a month. "Lead score" doesn't mean much for someone you sold a house to in 2019. If a field needs updating every week, you need a tool that updates it for you, or you don't need the field.


## Step 7: Keep it clean


Cleaning your database once is a weekend. Keeping it clean is about ten minutes a week.


Pick a time, like Friday afternoon, and do three things: add anyone new from the week (open houses, showings, new vendors), tag them with a type and tier, and archive anything that's obviously junk. Agents who do this never face a 4,000-contact cleanup again.


The other habit is writing things down when you hear them. When a client mentions their daughter is starting college, put it on their record that day. You won't remember it in six months.

## Who this isn't for


If you're on a team that requires everyone to use one shared CRM, your organizing happens there. You may still want a private copy of your personal sphere, since that's the part that follows you if you leave.


And if you're a brand-new agent with 200 contacts, skip most of this. Export your phone into a spreadsheet, add a tier column and a "what they do" column, and start calling. Come back to this guide when the spreadsheet gets painful.


## FAQ


### What is the best way to organize real estate contacts?


Get everything into one place first: phone, Gmail, any old CRM and your spreadsheets. Then merge duplicates, archive people you'd never call, and sort the rest into A, B and C lists. Add a close date and one personal detail to every past client.


### How do I merge duplicate contacts on my iPhone?


Open Contacts and look for "Duplicates Found" under your own card at the top. Tap View Duplicates, then Merge All or merge them one at a time. It only finds contacts with identical names, so check nicknames by hand.


### What is an A, B, C list in real estate?


A way of tiering your sphere by how likely people are to send you business. Your A list is the top 10% or so (people who've referred you or clearly would), B is past clients and warm sphere, and C is everyone else you'd still want to hear from you.


### Should I delete old contacts from my database?


Archive them instead. Archiving takes them out of your daily view without losing them. Delete only true junk like wrong numbers and duplicates.


### How do I export my contacts from my brokerage CRM?


Most CRMs have a CSV export in settings or an admin menu. If you can't find it, ask your admin or the vendor's support. Do it while you still have access, not after you've switched brokerages.


### How many contacts should a real estate agent have in their database?


There's no right number. A few hundred people you actually know is worth more than thousands you can't place. What matters is that your A and B lists are small enough to work every month or two.


## The bottom line


Your database is the most valuable thing in your business, and for most agents it's scattered across six places. Spend a weekend getting it into one list, merging the duplicates and sorting your sphere into tiers. Then spend ten minutes a week keeping it that way.
